data.title: What Investors Got Wrong About Uber Technologies Before The Drop
data.description:
Uber Technologies kept talking up robotaxis, AV partnerships and global delivery deals, yet the equity told a very different story. Investors who held Uber Technologies over the past year are down 23.2%, including dividends. If you had been deciding whether to buy in November 2025, would the mix of ambitious Lucid and Waymo collaborations, heavy AV spend and a sharp drop in net margin to 3.5% have changed your call?

Narratives are how investors here put a case on the record, with explicit assumptions about revenue, margins and the multiple. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

The Two Uber Technologies Stories Investors Had To Choose Between

The shares cost US$90.86 at the start of the period, so anyone looking at Uber Technologies then had to decide which story felt more realistic.

The bullish narrative saw fair value at US$106 and leaned on 14.6% assumed annual revenue growth plus a 13.7% profit margin in three years, supported by big AV and electrification partnerships.

The bearish view put fair value at US$72.92 and rested on a 9.0% margin assumption with a 44.7x future P/E, alongside concern that AV expansion with Waymo could strain returns.

What The Uber Evidence Tested In The Robotaxi Story

Uber Technologies pushed ahead with a US$10b robotaxi build out and a US$14.8b agreement to buy Delivery Hero, which both leaned toward the bullish growth story. The Q3 2026 report told a different side. Revenue moved to US$14,766m while net income excluding extras fell to US$512m and net margin slid from 49.2% to 3.5%. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The core assumption investors needed to watch was margin durability while Uber ramped capital heavy AV and deal activity. For any other stock with a similar pitch, investors can track whether net income and margin trends stay aligned with the promised uplift, rather than just focusing on new partnerships or headline investment size.

What Uber’s Lower Price Now Asks You To Believe

Uber Technologies trades at US$68.76, with the one year return down 23.2%. The Narrative’s Fair Value sits above the current price according to Ivoed, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the Narrative, and rests on how driverless economics play out.

To see the drop as opportunity rather than warning, a buyer today would need to believe Uber can stay the key demand aggregator even if autonomous fleets gain more bargaining power.

"The market is no longer debating whether Uber can become profitable. It is debating who owns the economics of transportation when the driver disappears."

One Narrative has put a figure on that disagreement. → See the Narrative with its higher Fair Value, assumptions and all

Looking Past Uber’s Robotaxis

Uber leans on software, drivers and delivery partners. Your rides and meals still depend on people showing up.

In other markets, a different super app is chasing the same everyday trips. It folds transport, food, payments and banking into one screen.

That platform earns not only from rides and deliveries. It also extends loans, handles savings and wraps in insurance.

As Uber refines its own ecosystem, this broader model poses a hard question. How much value eventually sits in the ride, and how much in the wallet around it?

data.title: Here's Why We Think Hour Loop (NASDAQ:HOUR) Is Well Worth Watching
data.description:
The excitement of investing in a company that can reverse its fortunes is a big draw for some speculators, so even companies that have no revenue, no profit, and a record of falling short, can manage to find investors. But the reality is that when a company loses money each year, for long enough, its investors will usually take their share of those losses. Loss making companies can act like a sponge for capital - so investors should be cautious that they're not throwing good money after bad.

Despite being in the age of tech-stock blue-sky investing, many investors still adopt a more traditional strategy; buying shares in profitable companies like Hour Loop (NASDAQ:HOUR). Now this is not to say that the company presents the best investment opportunity around, but profitability is a key component to success in business.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

How Fast Is Hour Loop Growing Its Earnings Per Share?

In the last three years Hour Loop's earnings per share took off; so much so that it's a bit disingenuous to use these figures to try and deduce long term estimates. Thus, it makes sense to focus on more recent growth rates, instead. In impressive fashion, Hour Loop's EPS grew from US$0.024 to US$0.047, over the previous 12 months. It's a rarity to see 96% year-on-year growth like that.

One way to double-check a company's growth is to look at how its revenue, and earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) margins are changing. While we note Hour Loop achieved similar EBIT margins to last year, revenue grew by a solid 8.0% to US$152m. That's encouraging news for the company!

The chart below shows how the company's bottom and top lines have progressed over time. Click on the chart to see the exact numbers.

Check out our latest analysis for Hour Loop

Hour Loop isn't a huge company, given its market capitalisation of US$51m. That makes it extra important to check on its balance sheet strength.

Are Hour Loop Insiders Aligned With All Shareholders?

Theory would suggest that it's an encouraging sign to see high insider ownership of a company, since it ties company performance directly to the financial success of its management. So we're pleased to report that Hour Loop insiders own a meaningful share of the business. In fact, they own 95% of the company, so they will share in the same delights and challenges experienced by the ordinary shareholders. Intuition will tell you this is a good sign because it suggests they will be incentivised to build value for shareholders over the long term. To give you an idea, the value of insiders' holdings in the business are valued at US$49m at the current share price. That's nothing to sneeze at!

Does Hour Loop Deserve A Spot On Your Watchlist?

Hour Loop's earnings per share have been soaring, with growth rates sky high. That sort of growth is nothing short of eye-catching, and the large investment held by insiders should certainly brighten the view of the company. The hope is, of course, that the strong growth marks a fundamental improvement in the business economics. Based on the sum of its parts, we definitely think its worth watching Hour Loop very closely. data.title: Is It Worth Considering The Caldwell Partners International Inc. (TSE:CWL) For Its Upcoming Dividend?
data.description:
Some investors rely on dividends for growing their wealth, and if you're one of those dividend sleuths, you might be intrigued to know that The Caldwell Partners International Inc. (TSE:CWL) is about to go ex-dividend in just 3 days. Typically, the ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the date on which a company determines the shareholders eligible to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is an important date to be aware of as any purchase of the stock made on or after this date might mean a late settlement that doesn't show on the record date. Therefore, if you purchase Caldwell Partners International's shares on or after the 23rd of November, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 15th of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be CA$0.136 per share, and in the last 12 months, the company paid a total of CA$0.06 per share. Based on the last year's worth of payments, Caldwell Partners International has a trailing yield of 5.2% on the current stock price of CA$1.15. Dividends are a major contributor to investment returns for long term holders, but only if the dividend continues to be paid. That's why we should always check whether the dividend payments appear sustainable, and if the company is growing.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Dividends are usually paid out of company profits, so if a company pays out more than it earned then its dividend is usually at greater risk of being cut. Fortunately Caldwell Partners International's payout ratio is modest, at just 26% of profit. With the recent loss, it's important to check if the business generated enough cash to pay its dividend. If Caldwell Partners International didn't generate enough cash to pay the dividend, then it must have either paid from cash in the bank or by borrowing money, neither of which is sustainable in the long term. Luckily it paid out just 12% of its free cash flow last year.

Check out our latest analysis for Caldwell Partners International

Click here to see how much of its profit Caldwell Partners International paid out over the last 12 months.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

When earnings decline, dividend companies become much harder to analyse and own safely. If earnings decline and the company is forced to cut its dividend, investors could watch the value of their investment go up in smoke. Caldwell Partners International reported a loss last year, and the general trend suggests its earnings have also been declining in recent years, making us wonder if the dividend is at risk.

Many investors will assess a company's dividend performance by evaluating how much the dividend payments have changed over time. Caldwell Partners International has seen its dividend decline 2.8% per annum on average over the past 10 years, which is not great to see. It's never nice to see earnings and dividends falling, but at least management has cut the dividend rather than potentially risk the company's health in an attempt to maintain it.

Get our latest analysis on Caldwell Partners International's balance sheet health here.

To Sum It Up

From a dividend perspective, should investors buy or avoid Caldwell Partners International? It's hard to get used to Caldwell Partners International paying a dividend despite reporting a loss over the past year. At least the dividend was covered by free cash flow, however. Overall we're not hugely bearish on the stock, but there are likely better dividend investments out there.

data.description:

  • The deal connects ResMed directly to a rapidly expanding virtual sleep clinics market by tying its connected devices and software to earlier detection and coordinated diagnostic services.

ResMed Investment Narrative Recap

To own ResMed, you have to believe its sleep and breathing health platform can keep pulling more patients into diagnosis and long term digital monitoring. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St leans on steady mid single digit revenue growth, high quality earnings and scope for margins to stay healthy. The VirtuOx deal fits neatly into that story by deepening virtual diagnosis and data capture rather than changing it.

In the near term, the key swing factor still sits with execution on supply costs, Astral remediation and replacing MatrixCare revenue, not VirtuOx. Astral corrective actions, freight and component inflation and the hole left by MatrixCare are the main operational risks flagged. If remediation drags or the refocused software portfolio underdelivers, the margin and earnings profile that underpins the current narrative could soften.

The VirtuOx acquisition stands out as the announcement most tied to this virtual sleep clinic theme. VirtuOx adds at home sleep testing and monitoring capacity that plugs straight into ResMed’s existing connected devices and platforms like AirView and myAir. That combination is intended to pull diagnosis earlier, then keep more patients inside ResMed’s ecosystem over time.

For you as an investor, the interesting angle is how this deepens the diagnosis funnel that analysts already view as a core catalyst. More virtual testing can support device and mask demand, while the digital tools are designed to sustain adherence and resupply, which matters for recurring revenue. The opportunity sits beside risks such as Astral and inflation, so the focus now is on how cleanly ResMed executes the integration and maintains margin discipline while virtual volumes scale.
